heading: How This Guide Works
text: How do you weigh all the rain falling on Earth, when almost none of it falls on a rain gauge? How This Guide Works Every page has one header bar like the green one above, telling you exactly which single idea the page is about. Nothing else happens on that page. Inside, follow the circled numbers in order. They run from low to high across the whole chapter, and each one depends on the one before it. Two characters will argue their way through all of this. Meet them now, because the whole problem is hiding in the gap between what they each know. Dot — a raindrop. I know exactly what I am: 2 millimetres across, falling at 6 metres a second, and I know precisely how many sisters I have in this cubic metre. Ask me anything. Core — the GPM Core Observatory, 442 km up. I know none of that. I know exactly one number: how much of the pulse I sent down came back. Everything else, I have to work out. Three more things you will see over and over: SPLAT!!! appears when an idea finally lands. TERMINOLOGY ALERT!!! boxes appear when a word is about to be used in two different ways by two different papers. And purple boxes are simulators — real physics, computed live, that you can grab and move. Psst! The colours mean things, all the way through. Amber is always Ku-band . Teal is always Ka-band . Blue is whatever we are trying to solve for, and red is what the radar actually measured.

heading: Measuring Rain From Space: Main Ideas
text: Measuring Rain From Space: Main Ideas Hang on, Core. Why is this hard? Put a bucket outside. Measure what's in the bucket. Rain measured! That works for the bucket, Dot. It tells you nothing about the next valley, and nothing at all about the ocean — which is seventy percent of the planet and has essentially no buckets. The problem: rain is both violently local and globally consequential. One thunderstorm cell three kilometres across can drop more water in an hour than the surrounding hundred kilometres gets in a week. So this is not a measurement problem. It is a sampling problem — and the instruments are not where the water is. A solution: look down at it. But how you look down matters enormously, and there are two very different ways. - A radiometer listens to the microwaves the atmosphere emits and scatters. Wide swath, whole globe, several times a day. - A radar sends its own pulse and times the echo. The difference is everything, and it is the subject of the next page. SPLAT!!! Then we will meet the satellite that does both at once.

heading: Why a Radar: Details Part 1
text: Why a Radar: Details Part 1 A radiometer measures a brightness temperature — one number, summed through the entire column of atmosphere beneath it. I can see that there is water down there. I cannot see whether it is at 2 km or at 10 km, whether it is frozen or melted, or where it changes from one to the other. A radar transmits a pulse and times the echo. And timing is the whole trick: every echo arrives with its own range attached …and range, from a satellite looking down, is height. So a radar does not return a picture of a storm. It returns a vertical slice through it, kilometre after kilometre along the orbit track. Same storm, same moment. The radiometer compresses it; the radar resolves it.

heading: The Core Observatory: Details Part 2
text: The Core Observatory: Details Part 2 The first spaceborne precipitation radar flew on TRMM in November 1997 and covered the tropics. Its successor, the GPM Core Observatory, launched from Tanegashima on 27 February 2014 — a joint NASA and JAXA mission. It carries two instruments at once: GMI, a radiometer with a 904 km swath, and DPR, the Dual-frequency Precipitation Radar. Now the orbit, which is a deliberate and slightly unusual choice: - 65° inclination — reaches well past the tropics into the mid-latitudes, where snow and shallow frontal rain live. - Non-sun-synchronous — the crossing time drifts. - ~93 minutes per orbit, about sixteen orbits a day. Why would you want the crossing time to drift? That sounds like sloppy engineering. Because a sun-synchronous orbit would see the tropics at 01:30 and 13:30 and never any other time. Convection over land peaks in the afternoon. Offshore convection peaks at night. I would have been permanently blind to the daily cycle of the thing I was built to measure. Over a month, the drift lets GPM sample every hour of the day at every latitude it reaches. SPLAT. NOTE: In November 2023 the spacecraft was boosted from about 407 km to 442 km to slow fuel use. The footprint grew from 5.0 km to 5.5 km and the swath from 256 km to 278 km. It is expected to keep observing into about 2030.

heading: Now You Try It: One Day of Orbits
text: Now You Try It: One Day of Orbits Run the full day. Then look at the white space between the amber swaths. That is my problem in one picture. I pass over any given place roughly twice a day, and a thunderstorm lives for about an hour. I will miss almost everything.

heading: The Constellation: Details Part 3
text: The Constellation: Details Part 3 So one radar is not the global product. It is the ruler that calibrates one. Because GMI and DPR fly on the same platform, every overpass gives a matched pair: what a radiometer sees, and what the radar underneath it knows is actually there. Those pairs train the retrieval used on every other radiometer in the GPM constellation — DMSP's SSMIS, GCOM-W1's AMSR-2, MetOp's MHS, and the ATMS instruments on NOAA-20, NOAA-21 and Suomi-NPP. None of those carries a radar. Every one of them borrows Core's. The merged product is IMERG — Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM. Property Value Grid 0.1° — about 11 km at the equator Cadence half-hourly Coverage 60°N–60°S full; 90°N–90°S microwave-only Early run ≈ 4 h latency — operational use Late run ≈ 12–14 h Final run ≈ 3.5 months, after gauge analysis Everything downstream rests on the radar being right. If Core's rain rates are biased, that bias propagates into the radiometer training, then into IMERG, then into every flood model, crop forecast and reanalysis that ingests it. The rest of this guide is about why getting the radar right is so much harder than pointing it down.

heading: Chapter 1: Self-Check
text: Chapter 1: Self-Check

heading: The Ambiguity: Main Ideas
text: A radar does not measure rainfall. It measures something related to rainfall — and "related" is doing an enormous amount of work in that sentence. The Ambiguity: Main Ideas Dot, I sent a pulse down and 29.0 dBZ came back. Tell me how hard it is raining. Can't. Not from that number alone. It could be half a millimetre an hour. It could be more than five. …those differ by a factor of eleven. The problem: the echo and the rain rate are two different summaries of the same population of drops, and they weight that population very differently. - The echo cares about D⁶ . - The rain rate cares about roughly D³·⁷ . Nearly double the power. That gap is the whole chapter. How we are going to prove it: not with an integral. With three raindrops in a box, and arithmetic you can check on paper. Then we will build a second box that gives Core exactly the same echo and rains eleven times harder. Psst! Real rain has thousands of drops per cubic metre. We are using three so the numbers stay small enough to follow. Josh would approve.

heading: Three Drops in a Box: Details Part 1
text: Three Drops in a Box: Details Part 1 Here is Box A. It is one cubic metre of air containing exactly three raindrops, of diameter 1 mm, 2 mm and 3 mm. That's me in the middle. Two millimetres. Pleased to meet you. Drawn to scale. Notice how much bigger the 3 mm drop is — hold on to that. Two formulas, and that is all the physics we need for now. Reflectivity is the sum of the sixth powers of the diameters: Z = Σ D6 [mm6 m−3] — sum over every drop in the box And rain rate is the volume of water passing through, so drop volume times how fast it falls: R = 6π × 10−4 × Σ D3 v(D) [mm h−1] where v(D) = 3.78 × D0.67 metres per second — bigger drops fall faster NOTE: Why D⁶? Because for drops much smaller than the wavelength, scattering is Rayleigh, and the backscatter cross-section of a sphere goes as the sixth power of its diameter. Chapter 5 is about what happens when that stops being true.

heading: Computing Z by Hand: Details Part 2
text: Computing Z by Hand: Details Part 2 Raise each diameter to the sixth power and add them up. That is literally all. Z = 16 + 26 + 36 Z = 1 + 64 + 729 Z = 794 mm6 m−3 That number spans about fifteen orders of magnitude between drizzle and hail, so nobody ever quotes it raw. Convert to decibels: dBZ = 10 log10(794) = 29.0 dBZ This is the number Core measured. It is the only number Core measured. Now look at where that 794 came from: Drop D⁶ share of Z 1 mm 1 0.1 % 2 mm 64 8.1 % 3 mm 729 91.8 % One drop out of three is making 92% of the echo. So when I measure 29.0 dBZ, I am almost entirely measuring your biggest sister. The 1 mm drop may as well not be in the box. Right. But she still rains. Watch what happens when we compute R. Your turn. Box A is not special. Drag any diameter and watch every line recompute.

heading: Computing R by Hand: Details Part 3
text: Computing R by Hand: Details Part 3 Same three drops. Now cube each diameter, multiply by that drop's fall speed, and add. v(1) = 3.78 × 10.67 = 3.78 m/s → D3v = 1 × 3.78 = 3.78 v(2) = 3.78 × 20.67 = 6.01 m/s → D3v = 8 × 6.01 = 48.11 v(3) = 3.78 × 30.67 = 7.89 m/s → D3v = 27 × 7.89 = 213.07 ───────── Σ = 265.0 R = 6π × 10−4 × 265.0 = 0.50 mm h−1 Half a millimetre an hour. Light drizzle. Now compare the two sums, drop by drop. Take the 3 mm drop against the 1 mm drop: echo ratio: 729 / 1 = 729 × rain ratio: 213.07 / 3.78 = 56 × Read that again. Make a drop three times wider and it returns 729 times the echo — but carries only 56 times the rain. SPLAT!!! Big drops are loud and small drops are quiet, but small drops still get you wet. Core only hears the loud ones. Your turn. The same box, through the rain-rate sum. (These are the same drops as on the previous page.)

heading: The Second Box: Details Part 4
text: The Second Box: Details Part 4 Let us now build Box B on purpose, to fool Core. The rule is simple: get Z to come out to exactly 794 again, using only 1 mm drops. Since each 1 mm drop contributes 1⁶ = 1, we need… Z = N × 16 = 794 → N = 794 drops Core's measurement is identical. Same 794, same 29.0 dBZ. Now compute the rain rate the same way we did before: Σ D3v = 794 × (1 × 3.78) = 3001.3 R = 6π × 10−4 × 3001.3 = 5.66 mm h−1 Box A Box B What Core measures 29.0 dBZ 29.0 dBZ What is actually falling 0.50 mm/h 5.66 mm/h Liquid water 0.019 g/m³ 0.416 g/m³ DOUBLE SPLAT!!! Eleven times the rain. Twenty-two times the water. And I cannot tell these two boxes apart at all.

heading: Two Numbers, Not One: Details Part 5
text: Two Numbers, Not One: Details Part 5 So what actually differs between the boxes? Two things, and the whole of GPM's Level-2 algorithm is built to find them. How big the drops are, and how many there are. Box A is few and large. Box B is many and small. D m , the mass-weighted mean diameter, is not the average diameter. It is ΣD⁴ / ΣD³ — the size of the drop carrying the average bit of water. It is weighted toward the big ones, which is what you want, because the big ones carry the water. N w is a normalised concentration. Loosely: how many drops there would be if they were all D m -sized. It is defined so that it does not drag the size information along with it. Compute D m for Box A — we already have the pieces: Σ D4 = 1 + 16 + 81 = 98 Σ D3 = 1 + 8 + 27 = 36 Dm = 98 / 36 = 2.72 mm — even though two of the three drops are smaller than that And for Box B every drop is 1 mm, so D m = 1.00 mm exactly. D m log₁₀ N w Z R Box A 2.72 mm 1.45 29.0 dBZ 0.50 mm/h Box B 1.00 mm 4.53 29.0 dBZ 5.66 mm/h One measurement. Two unknowns . That is an underdetermined system, and no amount of calibration fixes it.

heading: From Three Drops to Real Rain: Details Part 6
text: From Three Drops to Real Rain: Details Part 6 Real rain does not come in three neat sizes. It comes as a continuous drop size distribution, written N(D) — how many drops per cubic metre, per millimetre of diameter, at each size. Our sums become integrals, and that is the only thing that changes: Z = ∫ D6 N(D) dD R = 6π×10−4 ∫ D3 v(D) N(D) dD …same two weightings. Same ambiguity. Just smoother. GPM models N(D) as a normalised gamma distribution: N(D) = Nw f(μ) (D/Dm)μ e−(4+μ)D/D_ Look at what is blue . The two unknowns from the last page are the two parameters of the curve. Everything else is assumption. And μ, the shape factor? The algorithm assumes it rather than retrieving it — there is not enough information to do otherwise. So you've got one measurement, two unknowns, and a third parameter you're just… guessing? Yes. Which is why I carry a second radar. But first — play with the curve yourself.

heading: Now You Try It: The Drop Size Laboratory
text: Now You Try It: The Drop Size Laboratory Try this. Press Box A, then Box B. Watch Z sit still at 29.0 dBZ while R jumps about tenfold — the two boxes you just computed by hand, now as continuous distributions. NOTE: tenfold here, elevenfold on paper. A gamma distribution with D m = 2.72 mm is not literally three drops of 1, 2 and 3 mm — it has a spread of sizes around that mean — so the rain rate comes out slightly different. The effect is identical; only the third digit moves. Then try this. Set D m to 1.20 mm, press Lock Z, and drag D m up to 2.20 mm. Reflectivity stays pinned; the rain rate falls fourfold. The last readout is the one that should worry you: a is the constant in the Z–R relation everyone writes down as if it were a property of nature. Watch it swing by an order of magnitude as you move the sliders.

heading: What Core Actually Transmits: Details Part 7
text: What Core Actually Transmits: Details Part 7 Two radars share the platform, and from here on they are colour-coded everywhere in this guide. KuPR — 13.6 GHz, wavelength 22.0 mm. Essentially the TRMM design carried forward. KaPR — 35.5 GHz, wavelength 8.4 mm. The new one, and the reason this whole guide has a happy ending. Parameter KuPR KaPR Frequency 13.6 GHz 35.5 GHz Wavelength 22.0 mm 8.4 mm Peak transmit power 1012 W 146.5 W Beams per scan 49 49 Range resolution 250 m 250 / 500 m Range sampling 125 m (oversampled) 125 / 250 m Min. detectable rain 0.33 mm h⁻¹ 0.19 mm h⁻¹ (HS) Z min at L2 threshold 15.46 dBZ 13.71 dBZ (HS) Wait. The Ka radar runs at a seventh of the power and still detects lighter rain than the Ku one? That can't be right. It is right. At 35.5 GHz the same drops scatter far more efficiently — my wavelength is only four times your diameter. Hold that thought, because it is also about to cause me a great deal of trouble. Chapter 4 is the trouble. Chapter 5 is why it was worth it.

heading: The Scan Curtain: Main Ideas
text: Range is height. That one fact is what makes a radar worth putting in orbit — and it comes with a blind spot right where you least want one. The Scan Curtain: Main Ideas The idea: Core sweeps its antenna across the track, 49 footprints per sweep, each about 5.5 km wide at nadir. The spacecraft's own motion advances the scan forward. Stack enough sweeps and you have a three-dimensional volume of the storm. Within each beam, the echo is chopped into range bins — 125 m apart, sampled from 19 km above the ellipsoid all the way down to the ground. Most of those bins are empty air. The interesting ones are the handful that are not. There is one problem, Dot, and it is at the bottom. The ground is by far the brightest thing in the scene — orders of magnitude brighter than you. So the bottom of your curtain is ruined by the echo from the dirt? Several hundred metres of it. More near the edge of the swath. And that is the layer where the rain actually reaches the ground. That layer has a name — the clutter blind layer — and Chapter 8 will show you why it is a serious problem over the Western Ghats.

heading: The Real Scan Pattern: Details Part 1
text: The Real Scan Pattern: Details Part 1 That is the real thing, from the ATBD. Three different sets of footprints, and they are not all the same radar. - Pale blue — KuPR , 49 beams, the full swath. - Yellow — KaPR matched beams, pointed at the same spots as the central 25 Ku beams so the two bands see the same volume of air. - Pink — KaPR high-sensitivity beams, interlaced between the matched ones, with a longer pulse. Why two Ka scan patterns? Pick one. Because matching Ku exactly is what makes DFR possible — but a longer pulse on its own beams detects lighter snow. I could not have both in one beam, so I alternated. On 21 May 2018 the KaPR scan pattern was changed so that Ka covers the full swath, not just the inner 25 beams. Dual-frequency retrieval became available edge to edge. Remember that date. It is the single most important thing to know before you open a file, and page 7 of this chapter explains why.

heading: Three Heights That Matter: Details Part 2
text: Three Heights That Matter: Details Part 2 binStormTop — the highest bin with a detected precipitation echo. Above it, nothing. It matters more than it looks: the forward retrieval starts here, so an error in storm top propagates down the whole profile as an attenuation error. binRealSurface — the ground, found from the echo power profile together with the digital elevation model carried in the Level-1B file. binClutterFreeBottom — the lowest bin Core is willing to trust. And it sits well above the surface. The surface return leaks into nearby bins through the antenna's main lobe and, worse, through its side lobes. The effect gets dramatically worse away from nadir, and here is why: A 5 km footprint seen at 17° off nadir has its near and far edges well over a kilometre apart in slant range, so the bright surface echo smears across many bins. Everything below the clutter-free bottom is extrapolated, not measured. The Solver simply holds reflectivity constant from the lowest trusted bin down to the ground. For deep convection that is defensible. For shallow rain over mountains it is a guess about the exact part of the profile you cared about.

heading: Now You Try It: The Scan Curtain
text: Now You Try It: The Scan Curtain Try this. Slide the ray from nadir out to the swath edge and watch the blind layer thicken from about 400 m to over 1.6 km. Then this. Switch to Shallow orographic and notice how much of that storm is inside the grey.

heading: What Is Actually in the File: Details Part 3
text: What Is Actually in the File: Details Part 3 The curtain you just clicked on is, in the product, a set of arrays indexed by scan, angle bin, range bin and frequency. Learn these names early — they are in every GPM paper: Variable What it is zFactorMeasured the raw echo, before any correction zFactorNPCorrected after removing gas and cloud attenuation zFactorFinal fully attenuation-corrected — Chapter 4 precipRate the answer paramDSD the retrieved N w and D m flagEcho whether that echo counted as precipitation Every echo above the noise floor is converted to reflectivity and written out — including echoes below the precipitation detection threshold. zFactorMeasured having a value does not mean the algorithm considered it rain. flagEcho is what tells you that. Read the flags before you read the science fields.

heading: The Shape of the File: Details Part 4
text: The Shape of the File: Details Part 4 An HDF5 file is a tree. The top branches of a DPR Level-2 file are swaths, and they were reorganised in Version 7. - V06 had three: NS (normal, Ku full swath), MS (matched, inner 25), HS (high sensitivity). - V07 has two: FS (full swath, dual frequency) and HS. FS: 49 angle bins × 176 range bins, 125 m apart V07 applies the FS format to data from both sides of the 2018 scan change — but the data behind it is not the same. Before 21 May 2018: Ka/FS is missing angle bins 1–12 and 38–49. After: Ka/HS is missing angle bins 1–24. Same variable names, same shapes, silently different coverage.

heading: Where Every Variable Lives: Details Part 5
text: Where Every Variable Lives: Details Part 5 Inside a swath, the variables are grouped by the module that produced them — the same seven modules of Chapter 7. Once you see that, the file stops being arbitrary. Group Produced by What you will reach for ScanTime/ — Year, Month, DayOfMonth, SecondOfDay Latitude, Longitude — per ray, at the swath level — not in a group PRE/ Preparation zFactorMeasured, binStormTop, binClutterFreeBottom, binRealSurface, localZenithAngle, landSurfaceType, flagPrecip, elevation VER/ Vertical Profile binZeroDeg, heightZeroDeg, piaNP, attenuationNP CSF/ Classification typePrecip, flagBB, heightBB, widthBB, binBBPeak, flagShallowRain DSD/ Drop Size Distribution phase, binNode SRT/ Surface Reference pathAtten, reliabFlag, PIAalt, PIAweight SLV/ Solver precipRate, precipRateNearSurface, zFactorFinal, paramDSD, epsilon, piaFinal FLG/, Experimental/ various quality flags and fields still being evaluated The fully attenuation-corrected reflectivity was called zFactorCorrected through V06. In V07 it is zFactorFinal . Any script, tutorial or paper written before about 2022 uses the old name. If your read fails with a key error, this is why — and it is the most common first thing to go wrong.

heading: Attenuation: Main Ideas
text: The rain Core is trying to measure is also absorbing the pulse Core is measuring it with. At one of the two frequencies, it absorbs almost all of it. Attenuation: Main Ideas Small confession, Core. Every drop that scatters a bit of your pulse back to you also takes a bite out of the part that keeps going down. How big a bite? At Ku-band? Barely noticeable. At Ka-band, in a decent rain column, I will eat the whole thing. The quantity: specific attenuation k, in decibels per kilometre. Like reflectivity it is a sum over the drops — but weighted by the extinction cross-section rather than the backscatter one: k = 4.343 × 10−3 × Σ σe(D) σe in mm², summed over all drops in a cubic metre The consequence: what Core records at range r is the true reflectivity minus everything in front of it — twice over, because the pulse makes a round trip. 10 log10 Zm(r) = 10 log10 Ze(r) − 2 ∫0r k(s) ds measured true everything it passed through That integral all the way to the ground has its own name: the path-integrated attenuation, or PIA.

heading: Attenuation in Our Two Boxes: Details Part 1
text: Attenuation in Our Two Boxes: Details Part 1 Back to Box A and Box B. Here are the real extinction cross-sections, computed from Mie theory for liquid water at 10 °C: Drop σₑ at Ku (mm²) σₑ at Ka (mm²) Ka ÷ Ku 1 mm 0.031 0.331 10.7 × 2 mm 0.872 7.028 8.1 × 3 mm 5.941 21.856 3.7 × Psst! Notice the ratio shrinks as drops get bigger. Ka-band saturates — it is already near the limit of what a 3 mm drop can absorb — while Ku keeps climbing. Remember that; it is the seed of Chapter 5. Add them up for Box A (one drop each): Σσₑ Ku = 6.84 → k = 0.030 dB/km Σσₑ Ka = 29.21 → k = 0.127 dB/km And for Box B (794 drops of 1 mm): Σσₑ Ku = 24.5 → k = 0.106 dB/km Σσₑ Ka = 262.8 → k = 1.141 dB/km

heading: The Tie-Breaker: Details Part 2
text: The Tie-Breaker: Details Part 2 Now stack each box into a 4 km deep column and work out the two-way attenuation to the ground. PIA = 2 × k × depth: Z (what Core sees) PIA Ku PIA Ka difference Box A — few, large 29.0 dBZ 0.24 dB 1.02 dB 0.8 dB Box B — many, small 29.0 dBZ 0.85 dB 9.13 dB 8.3 dB Look at the last column. The two boxes are identical in reflectivity — and the Ka channel is attenuated by eight decibels more in one than the other. SPLAT!!! So the attenuation is not only a problem. It is information. The thing that is ruining my Ka channel is also the thing that tells the two boxes apart. Now you're getting it. Chapter 5. NOTE — be careful here. What separates these two boxes is mostly water content, not drop size: Box B holds twenty-two times as much liquid water, so it absorbs far more. Drop size leaves its own, separate fingerprint through non-Rayleigh scattering. The real algorithm uses both, and Chapter 5 keeps them apart.

heading: Now You Try It: Attenuation Through a Column
text: Now You Try It: Attenuation Through a Column Start where it opens — 10 mm/h through 4 km. The teal line has already bent below its detection floor before it reaches the ground. At 35.5 GHz, a moderate rain column is close to opaque. It is the Ka channel that dies first — the one carrying the size information. That is the cruel part.

heading: Hitschfeld–Bordan, and Why It Explodes: Details Part 3
text: Hitschfeld–Bordan, and Why It Explodes: Details Part 3 The classical fix. Assume a power law between attenuation and reflectivity… k = α Zeβ …substitute it into the integral equation, and it solves in closed form: Ze(r) = Zm(r) ÷ [ 1 − 0.2 ln(10) β ∫0r α Zmβ ds ]1/β Now look only at the denominator. As the integrated attenuation grows, the bracket shrinks toward zero — and the correction goes to infinity. So the formula works beautifully in light rain, where I did not need it, and detonates in heavy rain, where I did. And there is a second, sneakier problem: α has to be assumed before the retrieval starts, because it encodes the very drop size distribution you are trying to find. On the previous page, switch on the HB correction and drag D m up past 2 mm. The simulator fits α and β once, to a Marshall–Palmer-like distribution — exactly what a climatological relation does — and then lets you move the real drops away from that assumption. Watch the mismatch readout climb past 1 and the denominator collapse.

heading: Borrowing the Ground: Details Part 4
text: Borrowing the Ground: Details Part 4 The way out is to measure the total attenuation independently, and Core has an elegant trick for it: use the ground. The ground's radar cross-section, σ⁰, is a reasonably stable property of a given surface at a given incidence angle. So: PIA = σ⁰(no rain) − σ⁰(rain) whatever dimmed the ground, the rain took out — twice. This is the Surface Reference Technique. Hang on. Where do you get the "no rain" measurement? It's raining. That's the whole situation. From somewhere else. That is the entire art of the thing — and the reason it works far better over ocean than over your mountains. The SRT module builds up to five estimates for each channel and weights them by the inverse of their variance: Reference Where it comes from Works over Along-track mean of the last 8 rain-free footprints at the same angle bin and surface type, run both forwards and backwards everywhere Cross-track a quadratic fit of those averages across the 49 angle bins ocean only Temporal climatological look-up tables of rain-free σ⁰ on a 0.5° grid, by angle and season, split across 5 surface types everywhere Why the cross-track fit is ocean-only: the sea surface is smooth and statistically uniform across a 245 km swath, so a quadratic through the angle bins is a good model of σ⁰. Land is forest, then terrace, then bare rock, then reservoir, within a few kilometres. The fit does not behave, so it is simply not used. Every PIA estimate in the product comes with a reliability flag. Read it. The Solver certainly does.

text: Chapter 4: Self-Check

heading: Dual Frequency: Main Ideas
text: One measurement, two unknowns. You cannot assume your way out of that. You need a second measurement — at a wavelength where the drops stop behaving. Dual Frequency: Main Ideas If my second radar behaved exactly like my first, the second measurement would be redundant and we would have gained nothing. It doesn't behave the same, though. At 8.4 millimetres I'm not a small object any more. The idea in one line: because the two bands disagree, and because how much they disagree depends on drop size, the difference between them measures size directly. DFR = 10 log10 Z(Ku) − 10 log10 Z(Ka) Dual-Frequency Ratio. A difference of logs, so really a ratio. And here is the elegant part, which we will prove properly in two pages: in the ratio, the concentration cancels out. DFR tells you Dm (and nothing about Nw) then either reflectivity tells you Nw Two measurements, two unknowns, system closed. SPLAT!!! …and then, on page 5, we will look at what the curve actually does, and the happy ending gets considerably more complicated.

heading: When a Drop Stops Being Small: Details Part 1
text: When a Drop Stops Being Small: Details Part 1 Rayleigh scattering — the D⁶ law from Chapter 2 — holds when a particle is much smaller than the wavelength. The usual yardstick is the size parameter: x = π D / λ — small x means Rayleigh So for a 2 mm raindrop like Dot: Ku: x = π × 2 / 22.0 = 0.29 comfortably small Ka: x = π × 2 / 8.4 = 0.74 not small at all Once x approaches 1, the scattering goes into the Mie regime. The cross-section stops following D⁶, oscillates, and grows far more slowly. In other words, at Ka-band I'm not a tiny dot any more — I'm a lens. And lenses are complicated. NOTE: Every DFR number in this chapter is computed live from Mie theory for liquid water spheres at 10 °C — not from a fitted curve. The simulator validates against the Rayleigh limit to within 0.01 dB at small drop sizes. That departure is not noise. It is information — and it is the only thing in this whole problem that responds to drop size and nothing else. My Ku radar sees you the way physics-textbook Rayleigh says it should. My Ka radar sees you as you really are. The disagreement between them is my measurement.

heading: Why the Concentration Cancels: Details Part 2
text: Why the Concentration Cancels: Details Part 2 Four steps. Follow them in order and the result is unavoidable. Step 1. Split the distribution into "how many" × "what shape": N(D) = Nw × n(D ; Dm) ↑ a number ↑ a curve whose shape depends only on Dm Step 2. Reflectivity is an integral over N(D), and Nw is just a constant multiplier, so it comes straight out of the integral: Z(Ku) = Nw × IKu(Dm) Z(Ka) = Nw × IKa(Dm) ↑ these two differ — that is the whole point Step 3. A difference of logs is the log of a ratio: DFR = 10 log10 Z(Ku) − 10 log10 Z(Ka) = 10 log10 [ Z(Ku) / Z(Ka) ] Step 4. Substitute Step 2 into Step 3: Nw × IKu(Dm) IKu(Dm) DFR = 10 log10 ───────────────── = 10 log10 ────────── Nw × IKa(Dm) IKa(Dm) The N w on the top and the N w on the bottom are the same number. They cancel. Exactly, not approximately. DOUBLE SPLAT!!! So if you double the number of us without changing our sizes, both your echoes double, and the ratio doesn't move. Exactly. Which means DFR is a pure size gauge. Go to the next page and try to break it — move the N w slider as far as it goes and watch the DFR readout refuse to budge.

heading: Now You Try It: DFR as a Size Gauge
text: Now You Try It: DFR as a Size Gauge First, confirm Step 8. Drag log₁₀ N w from one end to the other. Both reflectivity readouts slide up and down together; the DFR readout does not change by a single digit. Then sweep D m slowly from 0.2 mm upward and watch the last readout — the one that counts how many drop sizes could have produced the DFR you are looking at.

heading: The Trough: Details Part 3
text: The Trough: Details Part 3 Here is the curve you were just moving along, written out: D m 0.2 0.5 1.0 1.5 2.0 2.5 3.0 DFR (dB) −0.01 −0.23 −1.21 +0.19 +3.21 +6.32 +9.09 Above about 1.5 mm it climbs steeply and behaves exactly as advertised. Below that, it does something awkward: it sags negative, bottoming out near −1.2 dB at D m ≈ 1.0 mm, before coming back up. Negative? Your Ka echo is bigger than your Ku echo? How? Mie scattering is not a smooth decline. Around that size there is a brief resonance where Ka backscatter is enhanced relative to Rayleigh. It only lasts a decibel or so, but it lands right where most of the world's rain is. Two consequences, both bad: - Every DFR value between about −1.2 dB and 0 corresponds to two different drop sizes — one below 1 mm, one above. - The curve is so flat there that a few tenths of a decibel of calibration error moves your answer by a large fraction of a millimetre. Light rain — most of the rain on Earth, and most of what falls over India during a break spell — lives in exactly that region. DFR and DFR m are not the same thing, and papers are not always careful about which they mean. DFR m is the measured ratio — it contains both the scattering difference and all the accumulated differential attenuation from Chapter 4. DFR without the subscript usually means the effective or intrinsic ratio, after attenuation correction, which is the pure size gauge. The curve on this page is the effective one.

heading: Which Way to Walk: Details Part 4
text: Which Way to Walk: Details Part 4 At each range bin we now have two equations and two unknowns — plus an attenuation term that has to come from somewhere. There are two places to start. FORWARD — start at storm top, work down. The attenuation above any bin is known, because you already solved the bins above it. The cost: it inherits the Hitschfeld–Bordan instability from Chapter 4, and the double-valued trough from the last page — at every single bin. BACKWARD — start at the surface, work up. Now the known quantity is the attenuation below each bin, anchored by the SRT's independent PIA estimate. The cost: you depend on the SRT being right, and on an assumption about the profile inside the clutter blind layer that nobody can check. The ATBD is unambiguous about which one wins: the backward method is preferred because it generally gives numerically stable and unique solutions, where the forward method may have two solutions at each range bin. In practice I do not commit to either. Chapter 7 shows what I actually do — I run the retrieval many times over and pick the version that best reconciles everything I know.

heading: What Ka Buys Above the Freezing Level: Details Part 5
text: What Ka Buys Above the Freezing Level: Details Part 5 Rain is not the only reason Core carries a second frequency. Look at what DFR m does in snow. Ku reflectivity stays below about 25 dBZ — weak, as you would expect from low-density ice. And yet DFR m runs several decibels, and grows steadily downward. That's aggregation. On the way down, snowflakes collide and stick. They get bigger, so the two bands disagree more and more. Which means I can estimate the phase-transition height — where ice becomes water — even in convective storms with no clear melting signature. Every passive radiometer retrieval in the GPM constellation needs to know where the ice ends and the water begins — the two have completely different microwave signatures. Core's Ka channel is where that number comes from. The radar is not just measuring rain; it is handing the rest of the fleet a boundary condition. TRIPLE SPLAT!!!

heading: Chapter 5: Self-Check
text: Chapter 5: Self-Check

heading: Classification: Main Ideas
text: Before Core can choose a drop size distribution, it has to decide what it is looking at. The evidence is the shape of the profile itself. Classification: Main Ideas Why bother? Because the microphysics genuinely differs, and the algorithm carries separate R–D m relations for the two regimes: stratiform: R = 0.401 ε4.649 Dm6.131 convective: R = 1.370 ε4.258 Dm5.420 Classify a profile wrong and you have applied the wrong physics to the entire column. Three categories, and the third one is the honest one: - Stratiform — widespread, gentle, layered. - Convective — vigorous, deep, lumpy. - Other — for echoes that are only cloud, or only noise, or that live entirely above the freezing level where the question has no good answer. And the single most useful clue I have is, of all things, an artefact. A bright horizontal stripe in the echo that does not correspond to more rain at all. Oh — the bright band. That's my sisters having a very bad few hundred metres.

heading: The Bright Band: Details Part 1
text: The Bright Band: Details Part 1 Follow a single snowflake down through the 0 °C level. Six things happen in order, and only the last two bring the echo back down. What happens Effect on the echo ① A large, loose snow aggregate falls slowly through the freezing level. weak — ice scatters poorly ② It starts to melt and acquires a coat of liquid water. ↑↑ big jump ③ Water's dielectric factor |K|² ≈ 0.93; ice's is ≈ 0.18 — a factor of five. ↑↑ ④ But it is still snowflake-shaped and large — it has not collapsed yet. ↑↑ peak ⑤ Melting completes. It collapses into a compact raindrop — much smaller. ↓ ⑥ Now dense and compact, it speeds up, so fewer drops occupy each cubic metre. ↓ Briefly, at step ④, the particle is the worst of both worlds for a radar: the dielectric of water with the geometry of snow. Hence a band, not a step. SPLAT!!! Where to look for it: the CSF module searches a window from 4 bins above the 0 °C range bin to 8 bins below it. Experience from TRMM: the peak sits about half a kilometre below the freezing level. Why a bright band is near-conclusive evidence of stratiform rain: A convective updraught is far too violent and turbulent to let a neat horizontal melting layer form. If you can see the band, nothing is stirring.

heading: What a Melting Particle Actually Is: Details Part 2
text: What a Melting Particle Actually Is: Details Part 2 Chapter 2 treated every particle as a sphere of water. The algorithm does not. It models each one as a sphere of three things at once: Pw + Pi + Pa = 1 liquid water + solid ice + air, by volume and tracks its bulk density ρ b in g/cm³ as the mixture changes. Phase P w ρ b Liquid 1 1.00 Solid 0 ≈ 0.10 Mixed in between see below A snowflake at ρ b = 0.10 is ninety percent air. Hold on to that — it is why snow is so hard. For a mixed-phase particle the ATBD sets the water fraction from a melting model, then gets the density from a startlingly simple empirical rule: ρb = √Pw That square root is doing a lot of work. Run it: P w — fraction melted by volume 0.01 0.25 0.64 1.00 ρ b — density (g/cm³) 0.10 0.50 0.80 1.00 A quarter melted and it is already half the density of water? The meltwater runs into the skeleton and collapses it. The structure goes long before the ice does. That is why a bright band is a few hundred metres thick and not a few kilometres. SPLAT!!!

heading: Mixing the Dielectric: Details Part 3
text: Mixing the Dielectric: Details Part 3 The dielectric constant of the mixture comes from a mixing rule — not an average, but one weighted the way scattering actually responds: (εb − 1)/(εb + U) = Pw(εw − 1)/(εw + U) + Pi(εi − 1)/(εi + U) U = 12.0 if ρb ≤ 0.09 U = 2.0 · e13(ρ_ if ρb > 0.09 A quirk worth knowing. Evaluate U on both sides of the boundary: at ρ b = 0.09 it is 12.0, and a hair above it is 2.0. The published formula steps there — two different regimes for fluffy aggregates and for denser particles, joined without a smooth transition. It is in the document as printed; if your own forward model disagrees with GPM at very low densities, look here first.

heading: Why the Echo Falls Back: Details Part 4
text: Why the Echo Falls Back: Details Part 4 Now follow one particle whose melted mass would make a 1 mm raindrop, all the way down. Two things change together. First its size. A low-density particle holding a fixed mass must be bigger: Db = Dmelt · ρb−1/3 Then its fall speed, which the ATBD gives in three density regimes: Vb = 3.3 √(ρb − ρa) ρb ≤ 0.05 Vb = 8.8 √(0.1 Db(ρb − ρa)) 0.05 < ρb ≤ 0.30 Vb = interpolate to the raindrop speed 0.30 < ρb ≤ 1.00 Put the two together for our one particle: ρ b D b (mm) V b (m/s) what it is 0.05 2.71 0.73 a loose aggregate, drifting 0.10 2.15 1.28 a snowflake 0.30 1.49 1.86 wet, collapsing 0.50 1.26 2.58 half melted 1.00 1.00 3.78 a raindrop It shrinks to a third of its diameter and speeds up five-fold, carrying exactly the same water.

heading: Conserving the Flux: Details Part 5
text: Conserving the Flux: Details Part 5 Here is the step that closes the argument — the N/N model, for non-breakup, non-coalescence. If no particle splits or merges on the way down, then the number crossing each level per second must be the same at every level. Speed up, and the concentration has to fall: N(Db) ∝ VR(Dmelt) / Vb(Db) go three times faster, and there are a third as many of you per cubic metre So by the time I am a raindrop, I am a third the diameter and there are three times fewer of me in each cubic metre than there were snowflakes. Which is precisely why my echo collapses below the bright band. Not because the rain stopped — because the targets got small and sparse at the same time. DOUBLE SPLAT!!!

heading: Three Methods, One Verdict: Details Part 6
text: Three Methods, One Verdict: Details Part 6 THE V-METHOD — vertical. Looks down a single beam. bright band found AND Z < 46 dBZ → stratiform no bright band AND Z > 40 dBZ → convective neither → other Two different thresholds, because a bright band is itself strong evidence — it earns a higher bar before the profile is called convective. THE H-METHOD — horizontal. Ignores the vertical structure entirely and looks at the pattern across neighbouring pixels, using a modified Steiner–Houze–Yuter separation. A pixel much brighter than its surrounding background is convective, whatever its own profile looks like. This catches the embedded convective cores inside an otherwise stratiform deck, which the V-method would smooth over. THE DFR m METHOD — dual-frequency, and a genuinely different kind of evidence. In the rain layer DFR m behaviour Why Stratiform small, flat with height Ku stays under ~25 dBZ, so there is almost no Ka attenuation to accumulate Convective large, steep slope differential attenuation piling up fast, plus non-Rayleigh scattering off big drops Why does the method use the slope of DFR m rather than how big it is? Surely the actual value is more informative. Because any fixed calibration offset between my two radars adds the same constant at every height. Differentiating with height removes it completely. Slope is free of a bias I cannot otherwise measure. DOUBLE SPLAT!!!

heading: Real Profiles, Real Data: Details Part 7
text: Real Profiles, Real Data: Details Part 7 Those are not simulations. Panels (a) and (b) are stratiform, (c) and (d) convective, measured from an airborne precipitation radar — and every claim on the previous page is visible in them. - In (a) the bright band is the obvious bump near 4 km, and below it DFR m in (b) is flat and small — barely 5 dB, barely changing with height. - In (c) the convective profile has no such bump, and DFR m in (d) climbs steadily all the way down. The marked DFR m (max) and DFR m (min) are the quantities the classifier actually measures: their ratio becomes the index V1, and the mean slope below the minimum becomes V2.

heading: GPM's First Snow: Details Part 8
text: GPM's First Snow: Details Part 8 And this one is GPM itself, three weeks after launch — overpass #000272 over the eastern United States, catching snow, stratiform rain and convection in a single 800 km stretch of one orbit. Region Ku reflectivity DFR m behaviour A — snow mostly under 25 dBZ several dB, growing downward — aggregation, not attenuation B — stratiform bright band at ~3 km near zero and flat below the melting layer C — convective 30–35 dBZ large and sloping throughout the rain Three regimes, three completely different DFR m signatures, one overpass. This single figure is why the dual-frequency classifier works. TRIPLE SPLAT!!!

heading: Now You Try It: Classify the Profile
text: Now You Try It: Classify the Profile How to read it. Sharp Ku peak just below the dashed freezing line → bright band → stratiform. High storm top → convection. DFR m climbing steeply toward the surface → big drops, heavy rain. Both traces stop where the signal drops below that band's detection floor — which is itself a clue. In heavy convection, Ka goes first.

heading: Nodes A to E, and the Phase Integer: Details Part 9
text: Nodes A to E, and the Phase Integer: Details Part 9 All of this has to be written down per range bin, and the DSD module does it by placing five nodes through the profile: Node Where A the bin nearest −20 °C — at and above it, Solid B bright band top C bright band peak D bright band bottom — at and below it, Liquid E the bin nearest +20 °C Between B and D the particle temperature is pinned to 0 °C whatever the air is doing. Between A and D the phase is Mixed. When there is no bright band — convective, or stratiform without one — B, C and D all collapse onto the single 0 °C bin. That is the whole difference in code: a melting layer with thickness, or a melting layer with none. And it is why Chapter 7 insists the classifier runs before the microphysics. Those five bins are the output of CSF and the input to everything that follows. The per-bin result is stored in DSD/phase, and its encoding is one of the neatest tricks in the product — a single integer carrying both phase and temperature: Value Means Example ≥ 200 Liquid, temperature = value − 200 °C 210 → liquid at +10 °C 100–200 In the bright band: 100 = top, 150 = peak, 200 = bottom 125 and 175 are the only intermediates used < 100 Frozen or part-frozen, temperature = value − 100 °C 80 → ice at −20 °C phase is not a continuous field. Plotting it on a colour scale produces something that looks meaningful and is not — a jump from 99 to 200 is a change of 1 °C across the melting boundary, not a change of 101. Decode it into phase and temperature first, then plot those separately.

heading: The Flags Beyond Three Types: Details Part 10
text: The Flags Beyond Three Types: Details Part 10 Version 7 carries far more structure than stratiform / convective / other, and the extra flags are usually where the interesting science is. Flag What it marks flagShallowRain shallow isolated and non-isolated systems, flagged independently of rain type flagBB, heightBB, widthBB bright band presence, height, and width (geometrically corrected for beam width and zenith angle) flagHeavyIcePrecip strong ice signatures aloft flagGraupelHail, flagHail graupel and hail; the hail flag is new in V7 and dual-frequency only flagSurfaceSnowfall built from a snow index combining DFR m slope, Ku maximum and storm top height typePrecip an eight-digit number, not a small integer typePrecip catches people out constantly. It is not 1, 2, 3. The leading digits give the major category; the trailing digits record which method decided it and on what evidence. If you write typePrecip == 2 you will match nothing at all. Divide down to the leading digit, or consult the user manual's bit definitions. So you've classified me. Now what? Now I finally solve for you. But classification was only one of six things that had to happen first — and the next chapter is the whole assembly line.

heading: Chapter 6: Self-Check
text: Chapter 6: Self-Check

heading: The Level-2 Chain: Main Ideas
text: Everything so far assembles into one processing chain. Six modules exist only to set up the equation that the seventh one solves. The Level-2 Chain: Main Ideas A main module calls seven sub-modules in order. They cannot call each other. Each one hands its result back and stops. Module What it adds to the ray 1 PRE echo power → Z m ; rain / no-rain; storm top, surface, clutter-free bottom 2 VER removes gas and cloud attenuation; flags the 0 °C bin 3 CSF finds the bright band; classifies the rain type 4 DSD assigns phase per bin; selects the N(D) and R–D m relations 5 SRT path-integrated attenuation from the surface echo 6 SLV the retrieval — everything above was preparation 7 TRG trigger variables, new in V7 Three algorithms share this framework: Ku-only, Ka-only, and the dual-frequency DPR algorithm that takes both single-frequency products as its input. The two single-frequency runs go first, in either order. The dual-frequency run goes last. Each processes one orbit at a time — but a whole month has to be processed as a unit for the databases to come out right. The ordering is not arbitrary: - CSF before DSD — the drop size assumptions depend on rain type and bright-band position. - DSD before SLV — the Solver needs the scattering tables DSD selected. - SRT anywhere between VER and SLV — it only needs clean surface cross-sections.

heading: The Real Diagram: Details Part 1
text: The Real Diagram: Details Part 1 That is the actual flow chart, colour-coded by module. Follow it from the top and every box is something you have already met: - Level 1 (echo power) enters at the top; PRE turns it into σ⁰ m and Z m and decides rain or no-rain. - VER (green) takes the environmental grid and strips the non-precipitating attenuation, giving clean Z m . - SRT (pink) reads its own database to produce PIA srt . - CSF (blue) does type classification and BB detection — and feeds the R–D m choice. Two things in that diagram we have not met yet. The cylinders are databases, not code: the SRT σ⁰ climatology and the DSD database holding the ε prior. They are updated offline, between processing runs, which is why a whole month must be processed as a unit. And at the bottom right: NUBF parameters. Core's footprint is about 5 km across. Rain is not uniform over 5 km — a convective core three kilometres wide sits inside one footprint alongside much lighter rain. Because reflectivity and attenuation are non-linear in rain rate, averaging over a non-uniform beam does not give the average rain rate. It biases the answer, and the bias grows with how lumpy the rain is. That is what the NUBF correction in the diagram is for, and it is one of the reasons heavy convective rain remains the hardest case even with two frequencies.

heading: Now You Try It: One Ray Through the Chain
text: Now You Try It: One Ray Through the Chain The same single ray is carried the whole way. At each stage, watch what gets added to it — not replaced. By the end, every marker on the plot was put there by a different module. NOTE: the single-frequency chain actually loops twice. CSF runs once on the non-precipitation-corrected reflectivity, then again on the Solver's fully corrected output before the convective decision is final. That is why a profile can measure 39 dBZ and still be called convective.

heading: The R–Dm Plane: Details Part 1
text: The R–D m Plane: Details Part 1 The Solver works on a two-dimensional plane: rain rate up the vertical axis, mass-weighted mean diameter across the bottom. Every possible answer for a range bin is a point on it. Two things are drawn on that plane, and the answer is where they cross. One crossing is the happy case. The next step is what happens when there are two — or none. The two curves: - The R–D m relation — an assumption, of the form R = ε r p D m q , chosen by the DSD module from the rain type. - The Z f contour — every (R, D m ) pair that would produce the reflectivity actually observed at this bin, drawn from the Mie scattering tables. Crossings What the Solver does one take it. Done. two prefer the solution with the smaller R and D m none take the closest point on the R–D m curve, and record the discrepancy — it becomes a cost term on the next page

heading: The Epsilon Sweep: Details Part 2
text: The Epsilon Sweep: Details Part 2 That blue curve is an assumption though. What if the assumption is wrong for my particular storm? It usually is. So I do not assume one curve. I try a whole family of them and keep the one that fits everything else I know. The family is indexed by a single adjustment factor, ε. The Solver runs the entire retrieval repeatedly, sweeping ε from 0.2 to 5.0 and picks the value that minimises a cost. In V7, ε is even allowed to vary with range rather than being fixed for the whole profile. The cost has four terms. Three for the single-frequency algorithms, all four for dual-frequency: Term In plain words a prior on ε "don't wander too far from the climatology in the DSD database" b PIA SLV − PIA SRT "the attenuation you produced had better match what the ground says" — one-sided when the SRT is saturated c Z f1 − Z f2 "and the answer should actually reproduce the reflectivity you were given" d Ka consistency "if you solved from Ku, the result must also explain the Ka observation" SPLAT!!! That is the whole retrieval. It is not a formula — it is a constrained optimisation run independently for every pixel in every orbit.

heading: What This Means When You Use the Data: Details Part 3
text: What This Means When You Use the Data: Details Part 3 Consequence one. precipRate carries different effective uncertainty in different regimes — tight where the SRT is reliable and the DFR is informative; loose over land, in light rain, where neither is. A single bulk error bar for a whole product is close to meaningless. Consequence two. The epsilon field is a diagnostic, not just an internal variable. It tells you how far the algorithm had to move from its climatological DSD prior to reconcile the observations. A systematically non-unity ε over your region is telling you something physical about the microphysics there. When a retrieved value surprises you, do not treat precipRate as a measurement. Walk back up the chain: precipRate → zFactorFinal → pathAtten and its reliability flag → typePrecip → flagEcho. Every stage of a seven-stage inference is visible in the file. Use that. One chapter left, Dot. And it is the one where everything I have told you starts going wrong at the same time. The monsoon. Of course it is.

heading: Chapter 7: Self-Check
text: Chapter 7: Self-Check

heading: Over India: Main Ideas
text: Over the Western Ghats, every assumption in this guide gets tested at once — and Box A and Box B turn out to be real places, in real seasons. Over India: Main Ideas The good news first. GPM's 65° inclination covers the whole subcontinent, and the non-sun-synchronous orbit from Chapter 1 samples the monsoon's strong diurnal cycle properly — afternoon convection over the plains, nocturnal convection offshore, at different local times across a season. The bad news. Three things go wrong, and they are the three things this guide has been building toward: - the drop size distribution moves between monsoon phases; - the rain that matters most falls inside the blind layer; - the surface reference degrades over land. Here's the thing, Core. In an active spell I'm a big drop in a deep moist column. In a break spell I'm a small drop in dry air. Same mountain, same season. …so a single fixed Z–R relation has to be wrong in at least one of those phases. Both, probably. Let me show you the numbers.

heading: Box A and Box B Were Real: Details Part 1
text: Box A and Box B Were Real: Details Part 1 Disdrometer observations over the Western Ghats show the drop size distribution shifting systematically between the active and break phases of the Indian summer monsoon: Phase mean D m mean log₁₀ N w modal log₁₀ N w Microphysics Wet spell (active) 1.30 mm 3.62 3.9 collision–coalescence in a deep moist column: midsize and large drops Dry spell (break) 0.92 mm 4.46 3.9 and 5.0 bimodal evaporation and breakup in drier air: many more small drops SOURCE. Joss–Waldvogel disdrometer at Mahabaleshwar (17.92° N, 73.6° E), JJAS 2012–2015; spells from IMD rainfall anomalies. Murali Krishna et al. , Atmos. Chem. Phys. 21, 4741–4757 (2021). The two N w columns are different quantities: the mean is what you compute with, the mode is where the histogram peaks — and the dry-spell histogram has two peaks. Note also that dry spells do not rain harder: mean R is 6.62 mm/h wet against 2.79 dry. What moves is the echo-to-rain relationship. Now put those side by side with the two boxes you built by hand in Chapter 2: D m N w Character Box A (invented) 2.72 mm low few and large Wet spell (measured) 1.30 mm lower few and large Box B (invented) 1.00 mm high many and small Dry spell (measured) 0.92 mm higher many and small Your toy boxes were not a thought experiment. They were the Western Ghats in July and the Western Ghats in August. SPLAT!!!

heading: Now You Try It: Wet Spell vs Dry Spell
text: Now You Try It: Wet Spell vs Dry Spell Press "Match Z". Both spells are set to the same reflectivity — the same thing a single-frequency radar would measure — and the true rain rates still differ by a factor of more than two. At any fixed reflectivity, dry-spell microphysics implies about 2.3 times the rain rate of wet-spell microphysics — and that factor barely moves with rain rate, because at fixed D m both Z and R scale with concentration. No single Z = aR b can sit on both. This is Chapter 2's ambiguity, in published numbers, over the terrain you care about.

heading: Rain That Falls in the Blind Spot: Details Part 2
text: Rain That Falls in the Blind Spot: Details Part 2 The windward slopes of the Ghats produce enormous accumulations from relatively shallow warm-rain systems forced up a steep escarpment. Those systems can be only two or three kilometres deep. Now recall Chapter 3's clutter-free bottom: a few hundred metres above the surface at nadir, over a kilometre near the swath edge — and higher still over rough terrain, where the surface return is messier. So a significant fraction of the profile that produces the rainfall sits inside the layer I am not allowed to trust — and the Solver fills it in by holding reflectivity constant. You're extrapolating through exactly the part I was falling through. And the surface reference degrades too. The cross-track fit from Chapter 4 is ocean-only. Over the Ghats the along-track reference must be drawn from rain-free footprints at the same incidence angle over a surface that changes character within a few kilometres. PIA reliability drops exactly where attenuation correction matters most — and cost term (b) from Chapter 7 weakens with it. Cost term (a) anchors ε to a prior from the DSD database. If that prior reflects a global or tropical-mean microphysics, and the Western Ghats in a break spell is running a bimodal, small-drop distribution, then the algorithm is being pulled toward the wrong answer by its own regularisation. The retrieved epsilon field over the region, averaged by monsoon phase, is a direct measurement of that pull. It is the first thing worth plotting.

heading: How This Gets Checked: Details Part 3
text: How This Gets Checked: Details Part 3 Validation over India leans on three independent sources: - IMD gridded gauge analysis — dense over land, the usual reference for monsoon-season evaluation. - Ground radar and disdrometers — these give the actual drop size distribution rather than an inference of it. - Inter-comparison between DPR, IMERG and the earlier TMPA products over the monsoon core region. The consistent pattern in that literature: satellite estimates capture the spatial structure and seasonal cycle well, and struggle most with heavy orographic events and with light rain. Two tails, two different reasons — and you now know both of them. Stratify before you compare anything. A bulk bias statistic over a whole season mixes wet-spell convection, break-spell shallow rain and stratiform decks — three regimes the algorithm handled with three different sets of assumptions. The interesting signal is almost always in the stratification, not in the mean.

heading: Opening a Granule: Details Part 4
text: Opening a Granule: Details Part 4 A Level-2 granule is one orbit, in HDF5. Everything in this book is a few lines away: import h5py, numpy as np f = h5py.File(path, "r") fs = f["FS"] # the full-swath group lat = fs["Latitude"][:] # (nscan, 49) lon = fs["Longitude"][:] rate = fs["SLV/precipRate"][:] # (nscan, 49, 176) hgt = fs["PRE/height"][:] # (nscan, 49, 176), metres ptype = fs["CSF/typePrecip"][:] # (nscan, 49) cfb = fs["PRE/binClutterFreeBottom"][:] # (nscan, 49), an index Note PRE/height. The file gives you the height of every range bin, already corrected for the slant path and the local zenith angle. Do not compute it yourself from bin numbers and 125 m. People do, and they get the swath edge wrong. Before anything else, print the shapes. Some fields in the dual-frequency product carry a trailing frequency axis of length 2 — Ku first, then Ka — and some do not: for k in ["PRE/zFactorMeasured", "SLV/zFactorFinal", "SLV/paramDSD"]: print(k, fs[k].shape) It costs one second and saves an afternoon.

heading: Six Things That Will Catch You: Details Part 5
text: Six Things That Will Catch You: Details Part 5 1. Range bin 0 is at the top. Bin 0 is near 19 km; bin 175 is at the ground. Height decreases as the index increases, which is the opposite of every intuition. 2. The fill value is −9999.9. It is a large negative number, not a NaN. Average without masking it and your rain rates come out catastrophically negative. rate = np.where(rate < -1000, np.nan, rate) 3. typePrecip is eight digits. Testing == 2 matches nothing. The leading digit is the category: major = ptype // 10000000 # 1 strat, 2 conv, 3 other 4. binClutterFreeBottom is an index, not a height. Use it to index the bin axis, and treat everything below it as extrapolated — Chapter 3. 5. The May 2018 scan change. Before it, Ka/FS has no data in angle bins 1–12 and 38–49. Any statistic you compute across the full swath will silently mix two different instruments unless you split on that date. 6. zFactorCorrected became zFactorFinal in V07. Every tutorial written before about 2022 uses the old name. Five of these six are version or geometry traps, not science. That is the usual ratio.

heading: A Curtain in Fifteen Lines: Details Part 6
text: A Curtain in Fifteen Lines: Details Part 6 This is the Chapter 3 scan curtain, from a real granule — along-track this time rather than across: import matplotlib.pyplot as plt s0, s1, ray = 2000, 2120, 24 # 120 scans, nadir ray z = fs["SLV/zFactorFinal"][s0:s1, ray, :] # (120, 176) dBZ hkm = fs["PRE/height"][s0:s1, ray, :] / 1000.0 # (120, 176) km cfb = fs["PRE/binClutterFreeBottom"][s0:s1, ray] z = np.where(z < -1000, np.nan, z) scan = np.arange(s0, s1) clut = np.array([hkm[i, cfb[i\ for i in range(len(cfb))]) plt.pcolormesh(scan, hkm[0], z.T, vmin=15, vmax=50, shading="nearest") plt.plot(scan, clut, "w--", lw=1.5) # the blind-layer ceiling plt.ylim(0, 15); plt.ylabel("height (km)"); plt.xlabel("scan") That dashed white line is the one to draw first, every time. Everything beneath it in my product is an assumption, not a measurement — and it is the part nearest the ground. Plot the line. Then decide whether your answer depends on what is under it. SPLAT!!!

heading: Where to Go From Here
text: Where to Go From Here The Level-2 products live at NASA's PPS (arthurhou.pps.eosdis.nasa.gov) and JAXA's G-Portal, in HDF5. 2A.GPM.DPR is the dual-frequency Level-2 file. Everything this guide referenced is in there: zFactorMeasured, zFactorFinal, precipRate, paramDSD, typePrecip, flagBB, binClutterFreeBottom, pathAtten, epsilon. Two habits worth forming: - Read flagEcho and the quality flags before the science fields. - When a number surprises you, walk back up the chain rather than arguing with the end of it. NOTE: the GPM/DPR Level-2 ATBD is the authority for what each field means. The user manual is the authority for flag bit definitions — which this guide has deliberately not reproduced, because they change between versions. So after all that — eight chapters, two radars, seven modules, a constrained optimisation — you still don't actually know how big I am. No. But I know it to within a factor that is useful, over the whole planet, every three hours, including the seventy percent of it with no rain gauges. And I know how uncertain I am, which is the part most people forget to ask for. …fine. That's quite good actually. TRIPLE SPLAT!!!
